_comment: Every statement this project makes about itself, with the state the recorded
measurements are expected to be in. `verify` checks this file against results/.
expect: 'holds'  - the statement is true and must stay true.
'fails'  - a known, accepted limitation. It is written down so that it
cannot be quietly forgotten, and so that fixing it is a
deliberate act that updates this file.
'not_exercised' - the profile cannot reach the condition.
A finding that flips in EITHER direction fails verification. A claim that
expected a real result but got 'not_exercised' also fails: an untested hazard
must never read as a green build.

findings.because: Append latency is long-tailed: inline merge_key holds both the shard lock and the appender lock while it decompresses, concatenates, recompresses and rewrites a key's whole run. The design document reports only throughput means, which cannot show this.
No single append should stall for more than 50ms. This currently holds at ci profile and is the guard that would catch inline merging getting worse.

Write throughput does not scale with writer threads. seal_shard takes the single appender mutex inside its per-extent loop and flush_builder takes it twice consecutively, so the write path convoys. Measured at 19% efficiency and negative absolute scaling at 4 threads. Every db_bench comparison in the design document is single-threaded, which is the configuration that hides this.

Reader::build materialises the entire key index on the heap -- one Vec<u8> per key plus a 2N-slot hash table -- so open is linear in key count and paid per process, shared with nobody. This is Bitcask's design, not the LMDB many-reader-process model the architecture claims.

Open cost is measured super-linear (20x the keys costs 30x the open), so it is not merely un-amortised, it degrades. Fixing this means a mmap-able, binary-searchable index shared through the page cache.
A 1,000-op durability window costs 25x throughput, because checkpoint() rewrites the whole key index rather than what changed.

There is no usable point on the durability curve: either lose everything buffered since the last checkpoint (512MB by default), or pay an O(nkeys) index rewrite per commit. An incremental checkpoint is the single largest piece of remaining work.
Every reader process must see a complete, self-consistent checkpoint state. This is the core safety property of the append-only design and must never regress.

metrics.because: A floor, not a target. The per-call timer is inside the loop here, so this is well below headline throughput; it exists to catch a collapse.
Single-threaded append throughput. The axis the design is built to win, so a regression here is the most serious kind.
Zero read errors across reader processes. Any nonzero value means a reader observed space the writer reused underneath it.
